hazards.definition: An unplanned loss of grid power to the home lasting four hours or more, from a local fault or a same-day system-wide blackout, and not caused by a named storm, flood, heat wave or winter storm (those are counted under their own hazards).

Population-weighted about 35 minutes and 0.7 interruptions a year. With a log-normal spread of durations (sigma 1.1-1.3, my assumption) about 3% of interruptions last 4 h or more: 0.7 x 0.03 = 2%, cut to 1.5-2% because repeat outages cluster on the same homes. System-wide blackouts add 1.15%: Italy 2003 (56M people) and Iberia 2025 (59M) among about 390M people over 25 years. https://ceer.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/C18-EQS-86-03_Benchmarking_Report_6.1.pdf

hazards.dwellingNotes: Typical urban home: a flat in a four-to-eight-storey block, often built before 1980, no generator, a shared cellar, frequently no car. Lifts and door-entry systems stop with the grid. Mains pressure usually reaches the fifth or sixth floor unaided; taller blocks, and many buildings in Spain, Italy and Portugal, rely on booster pumps or roof tanks, so their taps fail with the power (set the pumped-water option). Gas boilers and district-heating substations need electricity for pumps and controls, so heating stops in a power cut even when gas flows. Hobs are mostly electric or induction in Germany, France, Spain and the Nordic countries and mostly gas in Italy, Britain and the Netherlands. Air conditioning is rare: about 19% of European households (IEA 2022, search snippet), roughly half in Italy, a quarter in France, 4% in England. Electric roller shutters and stairwell lighting fail; emergency lighting lasts one to three hours.

evidence.claim: Unplanned SAIDI including exceptional events, 2016: Germany 12.8, Switzerland 9.0, Italy 37.1, Great Britain 38.4, France 48.7, Spain 53.6, Portugal 64.1, Ireland 80.1 minutes per customer. Unplanned SAIFI: Switzerland 0.20, Great Britain 0.48, Germany 0.51, Spain 1.09, Portugal 1.45, Italy 1.50 (France is listed at 0.08, which looks like a different definition).

Spain recorded 147 excess deaths (95% CI -35 to 330), 4.2% above expected, in the three days from 28 April 2025; ages 65-84 had 94 excess deaths (63 to 125). The surveillance system cannot attribute them to causes.
Spain: 35% of demand restored by 20:00, 61% by 00:00, 87% by 04:00, 99.16% by 06:00 and 99.95% by 07:00 after the collapse at 12:33 on 28 April 2025.
At least seven deaths in Spain were linked by press and police to the blackout: three from generator exhaust in one house, one in a candle fire, others dependent on powered oxygen.

hazards.notes: Probability excludes named storms (about 0.7% a year), heat-wave outages (about 0.6%) and winter storms; all four together give roughly 4.5% a year for a cut of four hours or more. The Iberian excess-death estimate works out at 147 / 48.6M = 3 micromorts per resident (interval -0.7 to 6.8) for a 10-16 hour blackout in mild weather: a check on the need curves, not an exposure entered here. No direct-harm exposure is entered; deaths in outages run through the needs and through side risks of coping.

hazards.dwellingNotes: Typical urban home: a flat in an eight-to-fifteen-storey block. AySA mains fill a basement cistern; electric pumps lift water to a roof tank that feeds the flats by gravity. When power fails the roof tank keeps running until it is empty: a reserve sized at about one day of normal use (rule found only in a Mar del Plata ordinance, search snippet; the Buenos Aires rule was not found), so a few hours to two days depending on how fast neighbours draw it down; after that there is no water and no flushing on any floor. Lifts stop, which strands old people on high floors. Most flats cook with piped gas (85% of Argentine urban households cook with gas, ENGHo 2017-18), which keeps working in a power cut, but newer small flats are all-electric. About half of urban households nationally used air conditioning in 2017-18 (47.1%, same survey); the city share today is higher (my guess 65-80%). Few buildings have a generator. Separately from any hazard here, the gas utility shuts off whole buildings for months after a failed safety inspection.

openQuestions: Heat window: the engine reads win.heat but the validator rejects that id, so heatWave entries carry it in extraWindows.heat (same shape as a window). Without it households without air conditioning get no cooling gap.

Default tick-boxes: the Buenos Aires preset should tick hot summers by default, because heat-wave power cuts (7.5% a year, the long ones) are counted under heatWave and removed from localOutage. Western Europe should probably default to hot summers and cold winters on, earthquake, wildfire and flood off.

Default settings by location: pumped water on for Buenos Aires flats and for Western European flats above about the sixth floor; air conditioning off for Western Europe and on for about two thirds of Buenos Aires flats; gas cooking for Buenos Aires.

Roof tanks: the engine opens the pumped-water gap as soon as power fails, but a Buenos Aires roof tank gives roughly half a day to two days of reserve. A baseline of about one day for water and sanitation when pumped water is set would fix this.

Thresholds: my localOutage event starts at four hours and storm events at six. If the United States file uses another threshold the probabilities are not comparable across locations, although each location is consistent with its own windows.

Calibration of heat: with my probabilities and heat windows the cooling curve gives about 39 (Western Europe) and 25 (Buenos Aires) all-ages micromorts a year without air conditioning, against about 100 and 29 observed. Western Europe may need the curve scaled up about twofold or the heat window lengthened; much observed heat mortality falls on moderately hot days outside any spell.
Cold severity: Buenos Aires cold is mild. I lowered coldShare to stand in for a severity discount; a severity scale on the warmth curve would be cleaner.

Dwelling: several windows differ sharply between ground-floor homes and upper-floor flats (flood trauma and displacement, storm displacement, wildfire). The schema has one profile per location; dwellingNotes say how to split them.
Sanitation windows here mean loss of water for flushing unless the basis says sewers; comms windows start when service is lost, net of cell-site batteries.
No channel fits queueing, search time and price jumps in a supply shock; I used financialLoss in dollars.
Building-wide gas shut-offs after failed safety inspections leave Buenos Aires buildings without gas for months. No hazard covers this; it matters for cooking and heating items.

Local prices: leave costs are in local terms converted to dollars (EUR 1 = USD 1.099; USD 1 = ARS 1,585). Item prices in the model are United States prices; a price index by location would be needed to treat them the same way.
